title: Charity is friendship (ST II-II.23.1)
hook: Thomas calls charity friendship with God

segments.voice: Yesterday, temperance: the right measure of the body's pleasures, which Thomas says gives a life its beauty. Your line was enough is beautiful.

"I will not now call you servants." Jesus says it at the Last Supper, in John's Gospel, the night before he dies. "But I have called you friends." A servant does what he's told without being let in on the plan. A friend gets told things. Thomas Aquinas takes that one word, friends, very seriously. Back on day three hundred thirteen, charity, the love that never falls away, was the greatest of the three. When Thomas comes to it, his first question isn't whether it's a feeling, or a duty. He asks whether charity is friendship. His answer is today's title.

Thomas borrows Aristotle's account of friendship, in three parts. First, not every love is friendship. People love wine, Thomas says, but nobody is friends with wine. You want it for yourself; you don't wish it well. Friendship means wanting good for the other, for their sake. Second, that good will goes both ways. A one-sided love isn't yet a friendship. Third, friends share something: a life, a work, a table. Now Thomas lays this over God. Does God wish us well, for our sake? Yes. Is the love returned? It can be. And what's shared? God shares his own happiness with us. Thomas points to Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "God is faithful: by whom you are called unto the fellowship of his Son." So charity, for Thomas, is friendship between a person and God. Here's what makes it bold. Aristotle doubted friendship could stretch across a gap as wide as the one between people and gods. And Thomas raises a sharp objection against himself: friends live together, and we don't live with God. His answer: we do, already, in part. Paul again: "But our conversation is in heaven." In that old English, conversation means the way you live, where you belong. Begun here, finished later. One more turn. Because a friend loves what belongs to the friend, charity reaches everyone God loves, even enemies, the way you'd care for a friend's children, for the friend's sake. Charity is not a mood. It's a friendship with a wide circle.
screen: `NOBODY IS FRIENDS WITH WINE.` · `GOOD WILL, BOTH WAYS, SOMETHING SHARED.` · `GOD SHARES HIS HAPPINESS.` · `BEGUN HERE, FINISHED LATER.` · then, large: `I HAVE CALLED YOU FRIENDS.`

segments.voice: Friends don't make speeches; they say what happened, what's bothering them, what made them laugh. If you pray, talk with God like that, plainly, about today, and then be quiet for a bit, the way you would with a friend. If you don't, bring to mind one real friendship and notice its three parts: wishing them well, being wished well back, and the thing you share.
Charity is friendship. For Thomas, charity is not only kindness. It's a friendship between a person and God, built on the happiness God shares. Today's word.
Your line: friendship with God. A friend, unlike a servant, gets told things. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics speak of charity as the greatest of the theological virtues, and the Catechism, following Thomas, describes it as the virtue by which people love God above all things and their neighbor for the love of God, and, with St. Teresa of Avila, describes prayer as a close sharing between friends.

notes: All Aquinas is paraphrased. Check: not every love is friendship (the wine/horse example), friendship requires benevolence, mutual love, and a communicatio (II-II.23.1); God's communication of his happiness as the basis, citing 1 Cor 1:9; the objection that friends live together, answered with Phil 3:20 (ad 1); charity extends to enemies as a friend's children (ad 2).
'Greatest of the virtues' and 'never falls away' paraphrase 1 Corinthians 13:8 and 13:13; confirm.
Aristotle's doubt that friendship can cross the gap to the gods paraphrases Nicomachean Ethics VIII.7; Thomas's question cites Aristotle but does not raise this point himself. Confirm the framing.
Douay-Rheims wording to confirm: John 15:15 (two fragments), 1 Corinthians 1:9 (fragment), Philippians 3:20.
'Conversation' glossed as 'the way you live, where you belong' (archaic sense); confirm.
howItsDone paraphrases CCC 1822 and CCC 2709 (Teresa of Avila on prayer as a close sharing between friends).
